description: CADS-dataset is a large-scale collection of 22,022 CT volumes with voxel-level annotations covering 167 anatomical structures for whole-body CT segmentation. It aggregates data from over 40 diverse sources spanning more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, collected between 2007 and 2024. The dataset includes both healthy subjects and various pathological conditions, with varying imaging protocols and anatomical regions.

name: CADS-dataset
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (Jan C. Peeken) contributed manual annotations. Expert review was conducted by an experienced radiation oncologist with 5.5 years in practice.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed through: (1) shape-based outlier detection using neural implicit functions to rank pseudo-labels by anatomical plausibility (Hausdorff distance between pseudo-label and shape prior reconstruction); (2) statistical flavor selection using Dice Similarity Coefficient and HD95 metrics with Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's variance equality tests, ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests, and post-hoc Tukey's HSD or Dunn's tests; (3) manual review of 65 test images from TotalSegmentator dataset by in-house medical professionals; (4) expert radiation oncologist review of segmentations from the clinical cohort.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: In-house annotation by medical research assistants and radiation oncologist; MIM software used for reference annotations in the hospital evaluation cohort
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multi-stage annotation process was used: (1) 167 target structures were organized into nine anatomical groups with specialized models trained for each group using high-quality annotations from established datasets; (2) specialized models performed whole-body pseudo-labeling to propagate annotations across unlabeled scans; (3) automated outlier detection of pseudo-labels in shape space using neural implicit functions; (4) multi-strategy label generation through an ensemble selection mechanism combining three complementary model "flavors" (GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, Shape-flavor) trained with different data quality-quantity trade-offs; (5) final label assembly integrating best-performing annotations. Manual annotations were also contributed by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset.
rai:dataBiases: Several biases are acknowledged: (1) Class imbalance — certain structures like uppermost cervical vertebrae (C1-C5) appear less frequently across the 22,022 volumes; addressed via oversampling with inverse probability weights. (2) Exclusion bias — the shape-based quality assessment excludes segmentations identified as low-quality, potentially eliminating cases with pathological conditions presenting atypical anatomical variations. (3) Limited coverage of certain structures — e.g., buccal mucosa appears in fewer than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations. (4) Pseudo-labeling noise — inherent inaccuracies in pseudo-labels from distribution shifts and limited initial training data. (5) Facial anonymization limits applications requiring detailed facial analysis.
rai:dataCollection: Data was aggregated from three main source categories: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes), NLST (7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and focused research studies; and (3) newly contributed images comprising 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. The collection spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of CT volumes from 40 diverse sources. Of the 22,022 CT scans, only 4,695 (21%) contain partial annotations from public sources; approximately 79% have no manual annotations. Sources include public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), research collections, and newly acquired hospital data. The dataset includes varying imaging protocols (contrast-enhanced and non-contrast), multiple anatomical fields of view (whole-body, head-and-neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine), and data from both healthy subjects and various pathological conditions.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Physical data collection
rai:dataLimitations: Several limitations are identified: (1) Exclusion of pathological edge cases due to shape-based quality filtering; (2) Coverage limited to head-to-knees (no hands, feet); (3) Brain mask is broadly defined to include all CNS components within the skull; (4) Optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; (5) Heart segmentation omits superior portions; (6) Rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent; (7) Trachea limited to air content without surrounding tracheal wall; (8) Vena cava needs more precise delineation; (9) Facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting detailed facial analysis applications; (10) Modular design with specialized models rather than a unified architecture; (11) Limited training data for certain structures (e.g., buccal mucosa in fewer than 1,000 scans).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Several post-collection manipulations were applied: (1) pseudo-labeling via specialized models for unlabeled scans; (2) shape-based outlier detection excluding the lowest-scoring 10% of pseudo-labels; (3) multi-strategy label generation combining GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, and Shape-flavor models; (4) rib segmentation refinement including connected components analysis, majority voting for rib class assignment, and costovertebral joint retrieval using vesselFM; (5) head region pseudo-label refinement with bounding box cropping to remove false positives; (6) oversampling with inverse probability weights to address class imbalance during model training; (7) interpolation of sparse 2D SAROS annotations to create dense 3D per-slice annotations.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step preprocessing pipeline was applied: (1) reorientation of all images to the standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention; (2) resampling to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution; (3) simplification of original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to both clinicians and researchers. By providing open-source data, models, and tools, it supports clinical adoption of AI in radiation oncology and diagnostic radiology. The dataset enables more accurate radiation therapy planning, which directly impacts patient outcomes. It also addresses healthcare data challenges such as class imbalance and potential biases while reducing overfitting risks.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended use cases include: (1) Training and evaluation of whole-body CT segmentation models; (2) Radiation therapy planning through rapid organ delineation; (3) Diagnostic radiology for automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes; (4) Anatomical landmark detection; (5) Cross-modality registration (CT-MRI fusion, PET-CT alignment); (6) Anatomy-guided image synthesis and reconstruction; (7) Longitudinal organ tracking; (8) Personalized anatomical modeling; (9) Large-scale population studies; (10) Body composition analysis; (11) Metastasis localization.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Multiple automated tools were used: (1) nnU-Net framework for training specialized segmentation models and pseudo-label generation; (2) neural implicit functions / auto-decoder for shape-based quality control of pseudo-labels; (3) vesselFM (a foundation model for 3D blood vessel segmentation) for rib costovertebral joint retrieval; (4) ANTs non-rigid transformation for brain structure annotation via registration with SimNIBS MRI atlas; (5) TotalSegmentator (v2.4.0) as a baseline model.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: All newly acquired CT scans are anonymized. Facial features in head CT scans are intentionally blurred using a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) to protect patient identity. The study received ethical approval from two independent institutional review boards.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of independent annotations per item; annotations are generated via pseudo-labeling pipeline with ensemble selection rather than multiple independent human annotations per item.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling in the collection process; the 79% unannotated scans are addressed through pseudo-labeling rather than imputation.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol for missing values is described; missing annotations are handled via pseudo-labeling (a separate annotation generation process, not imputation).
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance commitments are described in the paper.
null_reasons.inLanguage: Medical imaging dataset (CT scans with segmentation masks); no natural language content — inLanguage is not applicable

evidence.name: CADS-dataset : A large-scale collection of 22 ,022 CT volumes with full annotations for 167 anatomical structures, establishing the most extensive whole-body CT dataset to date
evidence.description: The CADS-dataset aggregates 22 ,022 CT volumes from 40 diverse sources, representing one of the most comprehensive repositories for medical image analysis to date. As the foundation of our CADS framework, this large-scale collection features voxel-level annotations covering 167 anatomical structures, serving dual purposes: enabling the development of the whole-body segmentation CADS-model and supporting further research in medical imaging.
evidence.url: Our CADS-dataset, comprising paired CT volumes and curated whole-body annotations, is publicly accessible via https://huggingface.co/datasets/mrmrx/CADS-dataset .

evidence.isLiveDataset: By making our large-scale dataset, our segmentation models, and our clinical software tool publicly available, we aim to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers alike.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: Our data collection strategy systematically consolidates CT scans and annotations from three main sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator [27] (1 ,203 annotated volumes with comprehensive coverage of 104 anatomical structures)... (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges... and (3) newly contributed images and annotations, comprising manual annotations of critical OARs on the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset [12], 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs, and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The geographic diversity of the dataset spans 16 countries across multiple continents, integrating data from over 100 medical centers collected between 2007 and 2024.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We aggregate our dataset from diverse sources, including medical imaging challenges ( e.g., Grand Challenge [36], MICCAI challenges [37]) and public repositories such as The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) [35]. Our selection criteria focus on CT scans that cover key anatomical regions throughout the body... Furthermore, three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (JCP) contributes additional manual annotations to the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Starting with a diverse collection of 22 ,022 CT volumes, where only 4 ,695 (21%) contain partial annotations from public sources, we develop a systematic approach to generate annotations for all 167 whole-body structures.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We implement a three-step pipeline: First, we reorient all images to the standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention. Second, we resample to a uniform 1 .5 mm isotropic resolution, which balances segmentation accuracy with computational efficiency. Third, we simplify the original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Our annotation methodology (Figure 2, detailed explanations available in Online Methods) first standardizes the data by aligning all images to consistent orientation and 1 .5 mm isotropic resolution. We then implement a multi-stage annotation process. First, we organize the 167 target structures into nine anatomical groups and develop specialized models for each group, leveraging high-quality annotations from established datasets. These specialized models then perform whole-body pseudo-labeling to propagate annotations across the remaining unlabeled scans
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (JCP) contributes additional manual annotations to the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset [12]... For this cohort, reference annotation masks were either generated using MIM software and validated by medical doctors, or directly contoured by radiation oncologists following standard clinical protocols.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (JCP) contributes additional manual annotations to the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset... To evaluate clinical relevance beyond quantitative metrics, we conduct a systematic expert review led by an experienced radiation oncologist (5.5 years in practice).
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We employ self-training through iterative model refinement, shape-guided quality control of segmentations, and fusion of the best-performing annotations from multiple segmentation approaches... We begin by leveraging vesselFM [107], a foundation model initially developed from 3D blood vessel segmentation, which has a strong inductive bias towards tubular shapes.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To ensure annotation quality, we implement two key safeguards: automated outlier detection of pseudo-labels in shape space using neural implicit functions [45,46]) (step 2), and multi-strategy label generation through an ensemble selection mechanism that optimizes structure-specific segmentation strategies by combining complementary models trained with different data quality-quantity trade-offs (step 3).
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We perform quality assessment on GT labels in 65 test images from TotalSegmentator dataset. Before detailed review, we correct obvious systematic errors such as mislabeled ribs and vertebrae. Then, in-house medical professionals thoroughly examine these pre-corrected labels along with the original GTs for the remaining structures. The review process involves independent assessment of all 104 anatomical structures, classifying each annotation as reliable or unreliable with documented error descriptions.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: A primary limitation of our approach concerns the exclusion strategy in our shape-based quality assessment. By directly excluding segmentations identified as low-quality from the training process, we potentially eliminate cases involving pathological conditions that present atypical anatomical variations... In the CADS-dataset, this class imbalance can be observed in structures like the uppermost cervical vertebrae (C1-C5) that appear less frequently across the 22 ,022 volumes
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: While CADS spans from head to knees, future work can extend to additional regions ( e.g., hands, feet) and achieve finer segmentation of anatomical substructures... Several regions require refinement: the brain mask currently includes all central nervous components within the skull, which may be too inclusive for certain applications; the optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; the heart segmentation omits superior portions; and the rectum appears shorter than its anatomical extent.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: The comprehensive nature of CADS enables various research directions beyond segmentation. On the technical side, it can support anatomical landmark detection, cross-modality registration, and anatomy-guided synthesis. For clinical applications, it enables a wide range of uses including longitudinal organ tracking, personalized anatomical modeling, radiation treatment planning, and large-scale population studies.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: By sharing the entire CADS framework publicly with its CADS-dataset, CADS-model, and ready-to-use tools, we aim to accelerate innovation and promote AI adoption in medical image analysis. CADS' clinical potential spans multiple domains: in radiation oncology, it can streamline treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; in diagnostic radiology, it can enable automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, we apply a Gaussian filter ( σ= 5 voxels at 1 .5 mm spacing) to facial regions. This relatively strong blurring effectively obscures identity while preserving the overall structural integrity required for anatomical analysis near the face area.
